conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. I understand you’ve been feeling unwell with cough and shortness of breath. Can you tell me more about your symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I started coughing a few days ago, and it’s been getting worse. I’ve had some wheezing and feel more tired than usual. My wife noticed I seemed a bit off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I didn’t feel hot, but I’ve been sweating at night. No chest pain or nausea though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You mentioned feeling 'off' since your last transfusion. Can you describe that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I felt restless, kind of different. Not painful, just… not myself. I thought it might pass, but it hasn’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ve reviewed your labs from clinic. Your white blood cell count is low, but stable. Platelets are also low, which we know from your myeloma history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I’m so tired?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. The fatigue could be from the infection, your myeloma, or low blood counts. We’re treating you for a possible lung infection with antibiotics started in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I got vancomycin and cefepime there, right? And levofloxacin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We’ll continue the levofloxacin. Your chest X-ray didn’t show pneumonia, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m wheezing a lot. Is that bronchitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very likely. We’re giving you albuterol treatments every six hours to help open your airways. You’ll go home with an inhaler for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my myeloma? Is that involved?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring it. Your oncologist advised holding lenalidomide and enoxaparin due to low platelets. But we’re giving you an IV immunoglobulin infusion tomorrow to support your immune system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had those before. They make me sweat a lot. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, diaphoresis is common and usually harmless. We’ll monitor you closely during the infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. What about my diabetes and hepatitis B?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re staying on your regular insulin and lamivudine. Blood sugars have been stable. No changes needed there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? I’ve had rib pain since the fall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re on your usual gabapentin and oxycodone. We’ll keep that going for comfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The wheezing is less, I think. Still tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. Your breathing sounds are improving. We’re going to start the IVIG infusion later this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any updates on the infection tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nasal swab for viruses came back negative. No flu or RSV. The sputum sample was too contaminated to use, so we can’t confirm bacteria. Blood cultures are still pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it might just be a virus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely a viral bronchitis. But we’re continuing antibiotics just in case, especially with your weakened immune system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing after the IVIG?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sweaty, like usual, but I’m okay now. Feels like it’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That’s a normal reaction. We’ll keep monitoring your labs. Your white count dropped a bit more, but that’s expected with your treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I’m glad. What about the blood cultures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still no growth, which is reassuring. We believe this was likely viral bronchitis. You’ll finish the levofloxacin at home—four more doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the inhalers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, albuterol for wheezing as needed, and fluticasone twice daily to reduce airway inflammation. Use them as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I see my oncologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re scheduled for bortezomib on day 14 of your cycle once you’re feeling stronger. Call the clinic if you develop fevers, worsening cough, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, doctor. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re discharging you home with instructions to rest, stay hydrated, and follow up with your team. Take care.
